metric.concurrency.assessment: Swift's concurrency design (structured concurrency + actors + compile-time Sendable/data-race checking) is one of the more advanced and safety-oriented concurrency designs among mainstream languages, comparable in ambition to Rust's ownership-based concurrency safety but achieved with less ceremony, though the ecosystem-wide transition to strict concurrency is still incomplete (an ecosystem/maturity concern excluded here).
metric.concurrency.normalization_rule: 0-100 scale, 100 = best-in-class concurrency design with full compile-time data-race freedom, lightweight structured tasks, and no unstructured legacy escape hatches; 50 = typical thread+lock/callback based concurrency; scored 78 reflecting actors, structured concurrency and compiler-enforced Sendable checking as strong intrinsic design, short of a perfect score due to transitional/optional strict-mode adoption and lack of certain low-level throughput primitives.
raw_observations: Swift has a modern, language-integrated structured concurrency model (async/await, Task, TaskGroup, AsyncSequence) introduced in Swift 5.5, built into the compiler and standard library rather than bolted on as a library.

Actors provide a language-level data-race-avoidance primitive: actor-isolated state is checked at compile time, preventing many classes of shared-mutable-state races without runtime locks in common cases.

Sendable checking and strict concurrency checking (progressively enforced, mandatory by default in Swift 6 language mode) give compile-time diagnostics for data races crossing concurrency domains, a significant safety-oriented differentiator versus most mainstream languages.

Structured concurrency (child tasks scoped to parent task lifetime, automatic cancellation propagation) reduces common resource-leak and orphan-task bugs compared to unstructured thread/callback models.
Global actors (e.g. @MainActor) provide ergonomic UI-thread-safety guarantees integrated with the type system.

Limitations: the migration from pre-concurrency (GCD, completion handlers) code to strict concurrency has been rocky, with legacy APIs and many third-party libraries not yet Sendable-annotated; full data-race safety (Swift 6 mode) is opt-in and adoption is still transitional.

No built-in green-thread/goroutine-style extremely lightweight concurrency primitive comparable to Go's goroutines+channels simplicity for raw throughput-oriented concurrent workloads, though Tasks are cooperatively scheduled and lightweight relative to OS threads.

metric.ffi_interoperability_design.assessment: Swift's FFI design is strong for C and Objective-C (module-based automatic import, no manual header duplication) and increasingly strong for C++ via native C++ interop, which is more ergonomic than most competitors' C++ bridging (which typically requires C wrapper shims). It lacks a general foreign-function story beyond the C-family ABI, same limitation shared by nearly every non-JVM/CLR language, so it is rated above average but not top-tier (no universal multi-language interop layer like JVM/CLR based languages).
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.normalization_rule: 0-100 scale, 100 = best-in-class interoperability design (e.g. seamless bidirectional multi-language ABI-independent bridging with zero manual glue); 50 = typical C-only FFI via manual bindings; scored 62 reflecting automatic C import plus native C++ interop as an intrinsic language/toolchain design advantage beyond typical C-only FFI.
raw_observations: Swift has first-class, low-friction C interop via automatic ClangImporter bridging: C headers/modules are imported directly as Swift declarations without manual glue code, and Swift can be exposed to C/Objective-C via @objc and generated headers.

C++ interop (Swift/C++ interoperability, stabilized in Swift 5.9+) allows importing C++ types/functions directly with automatic bridging of value types, templates (partial), and STL containers, though template/generic C++ code and complex ABI cases remain limited.
Interop with non-C-family languages (Rust, Go, etc.) requires going through a C ABI boundary (C shims), same as most native languages; no direct native bridge exists.
Objective-C interop is exceptionally mature (bidirectional, near-seamless) reflecting the platform heritage, but this is Apple-platform-specific rather than a general FFI story.
On Linux, C interop functions similarly via Clang importer and module maps, preserving portability of the underlying design, though tooling maturity differs (an ecosystem concern, not scored here).

unsafe pointer types (UnsafePointer, UnsafeMutableRawPointer, etc.) provide a structured, typed escape hatch for manual memory interop, more ergonomic than raw void* patterns in many languages but requiring explicit unsafety opt-in, which is a good design tradeoff.

No native support for calling into dynamically-loaded arbitrary ABI code beyond C ABI/dlopen-style patterns; no built-in support for calling into languages with incompatible runtime models (e.g. GC'd languages) without manual bridging.
